name: Coenzyme Q10
summary: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is a fat-soluble substance that every cell makes for itself and uses to produce energy. It isn't an essential nutrient, so there is no official intake. Statins lower its level in the blood. Trials of supplements found small or uncertain benefits for most uses, with the clearest signals in heart failure and migraine.
roles: Carries electrons in the mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy (ATP, the cell's energy currency)
Antioxidant in cell membranes and in the particles that carry fats in the blood (lipoproteins)

status.note: There is no routine test. Blood (plasma) CoQ10 can be measured, mostly in research: a review gives 0.40 to 1.91 µmol/L as the range in healthy adults. It is carried in the blood's fat particles (lipoproteins), so it is sometimes read as a ratio to cholesterol. Supplements reliably raise the blood level. This app has no CoQ10 marker.

signs: No signs of shortage are known in healthy people, because the body makes its own
Rare inherited conditions that disrupt how the body makes it (primary CoQ10 deficiency) cause serious disease and are treated by specialists
atRisk: People with rare inherited defects in making CoQ10
People taking statins: in placebo-controlled trials, statins lowered blood CoQ10
Older people: in a study of organs from people aged 1 day to 81 years, CoQ10 in most organs peaked around age 20 and then fell steadily
People with heart failure: lower CoQ10 in the heart muscle goes with more severe heart failure

signs: Mild stomach upset or soft stools in some people, though in one trial these were no more common than with placebo
high.note: No harmful level has been found. A safety review found low toxicity and no serious side effects in people, and called 1,200 mg a day the highest amount observed to be safe in trials. In a 4-week trial in 88 healthy adults, 300, 600 or 900 mg a day caused no serious adverse events. Extra CoQ10 doesn't seem to switch off the body's own production, and blood levels return to where they were after supplements end.

examples: Meat (the main source in usual diets)
Much smaller amounts in dairy foods, vegetables, fruit and cereals
foodSources.note: Usual diets give about 3 to 6 mg a day, about half of it as ubiquinol. Amounts in the same food can vary a lot between countries. CoQ10 isn't in the app's food table, so meals and the intake analyzer don't count it.

forms.name: Ubiquinone (oxidised CoQ10)
forms.note: The oxidised form. Like all CoQ10 it dissolves in fat, not water, so it is absorbed slowly and only in part.

forms.name: Ubiquinol (reduced CoQ10)
forms.note: Sold as better absorbed. In one small trial of 12 healthy adults, blood CoQ10 rose more with ubiquinol than with ubiquinone in the same capsules. A review warns that some makers' claims about absorption are wrong, and that how the product is made matters as much as the form.

forms.name: Solubilised or dispersed formulations
forms.note: Products made to dissolve or disperse better were absorbed better in studies. A review found that CoQ10 crystals that aren't dispersed cut absorption by 75%.

reference.noUpperLimit: EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) has set no reference intake and no tolerable upper intake level for CoQ10: it isn't an essential nutrient, because the body makes it in every cell. In 2010 EFSA assessed health claims for CoQ10 about energy, blood pressure, protection from oxidative damage, thinking, blood cholesterol and endurance, and judged that none was substantiated, so they can't be used on labels in the EU. Safety data come from trials and reviews instead: a review found low toxicity and no serious side effects up to 1,200 mg a day in trials, an observed safe level, not an official limit.

interactions.with: Warfarin and other blood thinners of the same type (vitamin K antagonists)
interactions.note: Case reports describe warfarin working less well while people used it. A small crossover trial in 24 people on stable warfarin found no change in INR (the clotting test) or warfarin dose over four weeks, but an observational study of 171 warfarin users linked CoQ10 with more self-reported bleeding. Talk to your doctor before starting or changing CoQ10 on a blood thinner; INR checks may be needed.

In placebo-controlled trials, blood CoQ10 was lower on all four statins studied. Whether supplements ease statin muscle aches is disputed. Muscle aches on a statin are worth raising with the doctor, who can look for other causes and options.
In trials CoQ10 lowered blood sugar and HbA1c slightly, more in people with diabetes. Worth mentioning to the doctor when blood sugar treatment is being adjusted.
Trials didn't show a clear fall in blood pressure with CoQ10, and whether it adds to blood pressure medicines hasn't been well studied. Mention it to the doctor treating your blood pressure.

cautions: CoQ10 is studied in heart failure only as an add-on to medical treatment, never instead of it.
Products vary: how CoQ10 is made and dispersed changes how much is absorbed, and some absorption claims on labels are wrong.
Little is known about safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children.
EU rules don't allow health claims for CoQ10 on labels, because EFSA found none substantiated.

commonUses: May support energy production in cells, which happens in the mitochondria.
May support the mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy, as people age.
May help skin look younger and smoother.
May support heart health, especially in people with heart failure who are already being treated.

origin: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is a fat-soluble substance that every cell makes and uses in the mitochondria to produce energy. Supplements are mostly made by fermenting yeast or bacteria, or by chemical synthesis; ubiquinol is the reduced form of CoQ10 and ubiquinone is the oxidised form.
dosage: No official reference intake or tolerable upper intake level exists for CoQ10, because it is not an essential nutrient: the body makes it. In 2010 EFSA judged that health claims for CoQ10 were not substantiated. A safety review called 1,200 mg a day the highest amount observed to be safe in trials; this is not an official limit.
An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 100 mg a day, often as ubiquinol. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

On a label, check which form is used (ubiquinone or ubiquinol) and how much CoQ10 is in one serving. CoQ10 dissolves in fat, and how a product is made affects absorption, so claims about a form are not always reliable. People on warfarin should talk to their doctor first.

foodAmounts.verdict: No. Meat is the main food source of CoQ10, with smaller amounts in fish, nuts and oils, and usual diets supply roughly 3 to 6 mg a day, far less than the 100 mg used in supplements. Food alone is not a practical way to reach that amount.
foodAmounts.notChecked: CoQ10 is not measured in the food table used by this app, so no per-food amounts are listed. The 3 to 6 mg figure comes from Danish diet studies.
